title: Division: sharing vs grouping
examples: When do I know if I should share or group?
What is the difference between a remainder of zero and a remainder of one?
How does division relate to multiplication?

explain.say: Today we learn about division. Division can mean two different things. Sometimes it means sharing things equally among friends. Another time it means putting things into equal groups.
Imagine you have ten sweets to share among two friends. You give one to each friend until none are left. This is sharing equally. You are dividing the total amount by the number of people.
Now, let us try grouping. If you have ten sweets and you want to put them into groups of two. You count how many groups you can make. This is finding how many groups fit.
Sometimes when we divide, things are left over. These leftovers are called remainders. A remainder tells us what is left after sharing or grouping as much as possible.

items: Tells what is left after sharing

explain.say: Division is the opposite of multiplication. If you know that three groups of four equals twelve, then twelve divided by four must equal three. They undo each other.

faq.q: When should I use sharing versus grouping?
faq.a: If the problem says sharing among people, you are sharing. If it says putting into equal groups, you are grouping. You can look for keywords to help you decide.
asks: What tells me which way to divide?

faq.q: What does a remainder of zero mean?
faq.a: A remainder of zero means that everything was shared or grouped perfectly. There are no items left over at all.
asks: Does zero remainder mean it divides exactly?
What if there are no leftovers?

faq.q: How do I check if my division is correct?
faq.a: You can check by multiplying the answer by the divisor. Then you add the remainder to that product. It should equal your starting total.
asks: What is the inverse of division?

faq.q: Is grouping always the same as sharing?
faq.a: Not always. Sharing is about dividing a total amount by the number of groups. Grouping is about seeing how many groups of a certain size fit into the total amount.
asks: Are sharing and grouping the same thing?
Do they always give the same answer?

faq.q: What if the remainder is bigger than the group size?
faq.a: The remainder must always be smaller than the number you are grouping by. If it is not, you have not divided completely.
asks: What is the rule for the remainder?

facts: Division can be understood as splitting a total into equal parts.
If you divide a number by itself, the answer is always one.
The remainder must always be less than the divisor.
Division is the inverse operation of multiplication.

quiz.say: If you have 15 stickers and you put them into groups of 3, how many groups do you make?
quiz.why: This is grouping, so you find how many groups of 3 fit into 15. Five groups fit perfectly.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you only found one group size, not the total number of groups.
wrong.1: This is wrong because you multiplied 3 by 3, instead of dividing 15 by 3.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you wrote the original total number, not the answer to the division.

quiz.say: A teacher has 23 pencils to share equally among 5 students. How many pencils will each student get, and what is left over?
quiz.why: This is sharing. Each student gets 4 pencils, and 3 pencils are left over because 5 groups of 4 is 20, and 23 minus 20 is 3.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you divided by 5, so the remainder cannot be 5 or more.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the remainder cannot be bigger than the number of groups you are making.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the remainder must always be smaller than the number of students you are sharing with.

quiz.say: Which multiplication fact correctly shows that 20 divided by 5 equals 4?
quiz.why: Division undoes multiplication. If 4 groups of 5 make 20, then 20 divided by 5 must be 4.

wrong.0: This is wrong because addition is not the inverse operation for division.
wrong.1: This is wrong because subtraction is also not the inverse operation for division.
wrong.3: This is wrong because while the numbers are correct, the order matters when thinking about the inverse relationship.
